presenceLabel: Six Nations cession or claim in this area (contested)
presenceNote: 1768 is the Treaty of Fort Stanwix (5 Nov 1768). 1784 is the second Fort Stanwix treaty, in which the Six Nations yielded claims west of a Pennsylvania–New York line (1789 Fort Harmar renewed it). The Kentucky area is a legal claim sold to the Crown (a general area by treaty cession, not where people lived, not a legal boundary); Mingo (Ohio Iroquois) lived on the upper Ohio, north of the river. The route through New York and Pennsylvania is described in text only; nothing is drawn or filled outside Kentucky.
overlapNote: The whole Kentucky cession overlaps the Cherokee (Hard Labour 14 Oct 1768 and Lochaber 1770 drew Cherokee lines in the same land; Johnson wrote that he never found the Cherokee claiming north of the Tennessee, while Stuart complained), the Shawnee (present but not signers; contested until Camp Charlotte 1774) and the Chickasaw in the far west. The Board of Trade had told Johnson to stop at the Kanawha; the Six Nations insisted on the Tennessee. The Lenape and Shawnee were named in the deed as dependents, which they denied.
basis: Treaty text (Stanwix 1768 deed and proceedings) plus the Ohio River centreline (Natural Earth). County list is a clip of the deed’s Ohio River call, not a surveyed boundary. The Susquehanna-Delaware-Wood Creek legs are outside the map window and are described, not drawn. Native Land Digital data was not used.

eras.label: 5 Nov 1768 · Fort Stanwix: the Line of Property
eras.text: On 5 Nov 1768 six Six Nations signers sold the Crown a huge tract at Fort Stanwix (Rome, NY) for £10,460 7s 3d in goods and money. The deed line began at the mouth of the Cherokee (Tennessee) River, ran up the south side of the Ohio to Kittanning, then across Pennsylvania and New York to Wood Creek near Fort Stanwix. Everything east of it to the colonies was ceded. In Kentucky that is everything east of the Tennessee River. The hatched area is a general area by treaty cession, not where people lived, clipped to Kentucky (its south edge is the modern state line, not a treaty edge) and not a legal boundary. The Ohio River is drawn solid inside Kentucky and dashed beyond. The Cherokee and Shawnee had not agreed, and the Board of Trade had wanted the line to stop at the Kanawha.

eras.label: 1774–1784 · Contested claim
eras.text: The cession stayed disputed. The Cherokee had their own line from Hard Labour (14 Oct 1768) and Lochaber (1770); the Shawnee accepted the Ohio River only at Camp Charlotte (19 Oct 1774), after Dunmore’s War. Historians question how real Six Nations control was: Anderson calls it an “illusion of control” resting on the Mingo, Shawnee and Delaware being willing to cooperate. The Six Nations’ claim rested on the 1600s wars and the Covenant Chain, which the Virginia commissioners at Lancaster (1744) called land “altogether deserted”. Shown softly: a contested claim by cession, not where people lived.

eras.label: 1784–1789 · Claims given up
eras.text: At the second Fort Stanwix treaty (Oct 1784) the Six Nations yielded claims west of a line from the Niagara area south to the Pennsylvania border and along Pennsylvania’s western edge to the Ohio. The Buffalo Creek council refused to ratify it and the Ohio-country tribes rejected it. Fort Harmar (9 Jan 1789, Mohawks absent) renewed the same boundary. Neither treaty has a Kentucky line, so nothing is drawn.

The deed line begins at the mouth of the "Cherokee or Hogohege River" (Tennessee River) where it empties into the Ohio (Tennessee mouth 37.067, -88.565 per Wikipedia) and runs up the south side of the Ohio. Drawn on the Natural Earth Ohio River centreline from the Tennessee mouth to the eastern end of Kentucky near the Big Sandy mouth; the river is the Kentucky border here, so the line is also the state edge.
